name: Italian Game
tagline: The oldest opening in chess — and still one of the very best.

introduction.title: Welcome to the Italian Game
body: The Italian Game begins 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4. It is one of the oldest recorded openings in chess — analysed by Italian masters like Greco back in the 1600s — and it has never gone out of fashion. Today you'll see it in the games of complete beginners and in World Championship matches alike.

The whole opening is built around one idea: the bishop on c4 stares straight at f7. That square is the weakest point in Black's position because, at the start of the game, only the king defends it. Everything White does flows from that pressure — sometimes a slow build-up, sometimes an all-out sacrifice on f7.

This course will take you from the very first moves to a confident, trained repertoire. You'll learn the calm positional lines AND the wild gambits, understand the plans behind them, then drill them until they're automatic. By the end, the Italian will feel like home.

points.t: The bishop on c4 and the knight (via g5 or e5) gang up on f7. Even when you don't sacrifice there, the threat shapes the whole game — it ties Black down.

points.h: Two ways to play the centre
points.t: Either build a big pawn centre with c3 then d4 (the classical Giuoco Piano), or keep it solid and slow with d3 (the modern Giuoco Pianissimo that top players love). Pick the style that suits you.
Knights to f3/c3, bishop to c4, castle kingside, rooks to the centre. The Italian rewards getting your pieces out quickly and harmoniously.
The Evans Gambit (b4) and the Fried Liver (Nxf7) sacrifice material to drag the king out and attack. They're not just tricks — they're principled, time-tested attacking systems.
After c3 and d4 in the Giuoco Piano, White gets two big centre pawns. They cramp Black and give your pieces room — but you must be ready to defend them once the position opens.
In the Pianissimo, White keeps pawns on d3 and e4. It's modest but rock-solid, and it lets White manoeuvre slowly (the famous Nbd2–f1–g3 knight tour) before striking.
In the Evans, Fried Liver, Max Lange and Scotch Gambit, the centre opens early. Pawn structure matters less than piece activity and king safety — you're playing for the attack.
In the Evans or Fried Liver you've invested material for time. Don't dawdle — if you let Black consolidate and untangle, you're just down a pawn or piece.
Beginners often develop on autopilot and miss that f7 is hanging by a thread. Always check whether Bxf7+ or Ng5 ideas are in the air.
Especially as Black, snatching the e4-pawn or b-pawn too greedily hands White a huge lead in development. Material isn't worth much if your king is stuck in the centre.

points.h: Trading into a worse endgame when ahead in development
points.t: If you have the initiative, keep pieces ON. Trading helps the side that's cramped or behind in development.

Main Line (c3 + d4 centre).name: Main Line (c3 + d4 centre)
notes: 1.e4 — open the king's pawn, free the bishop and queen, plant a flag in the centre. The most popular move on the planet, and for good reason.
1...e5 — Black says 'you want the centre? so do I.' Classical and symmetrical… for now.
2.Nf3 — develop and poke the e5-pawn. Development WITH a threat is the dream.
2...Nc6 — defends e5 and develops. Textbook.
3.Bc4 — the Italian bishop, sniping at f7 — the only square the enemy king guards all by himself.
3...Bc5 — Black copies you and aims at YOUR f2. A bishop staring contest.
4.c3 — looks shy, hits hard: it's prepping d4 to build a giant centre.
4...Nf6 — develops and jabs at e4. Black pokes back.
5.d4 — boom. The big break. White grabs the centre and opens lines.
5...exd4 — Black takes; letting dxe5 happen would just be sad.
6.cxd4 — recapture, and now the dream pawns on d4+e4 are up. A textbook centre.
6...Bb4+ — a cheeky check to develop with tempo before White gets comfy.
7.Nc3 — block the check by developing. Two jobs, one knight.
7...Nxe4!? — the critical grab. Black snatches e4 and dares you to prove the gambit. Theory gets spicy here.
8.O-O — castle, king safe, rooks connected. Never attack with your king stuck in the middle.
8...Bxc3 — Black trades the pinned knight before it makes trouble.
9.d5! — the key move. Kick the c6-knight and rip open lines. You're playing for the attack, not the pawn.
9...Bf6 — the bishop retreats somewhere safe and useful instead of getting trapped.
10.Re1 — slam the rook on the e-file, right at that loose e4-knight. Pressure, pressure.
10...Ne7 — the knight scurries back to defend; Black untangles carefully.
11.Rxe4 — win the knight back; the dust settles into a rich position with your pieces buzzing.
11...d6 — Black solidifies and gives the c8-bishop a window.
12.Bg5 — develop the last bishop with a pin on e7. Annoying for Black.
12...Bxg5 — Black trades off the pinning bishop to ease the pressure.
13.Nxg5 — recapture, and the knight lands on g5 eyeing f7 and h7. Sneaky.
13...O-O — Black finally castles into safety.

14.Nxh7! — a little tactical bonus: the knight grabs h7. White emerges with an extra pawn and a pleasant, active position. The d5-pawn and active rooks give you a comfortable pull into the middlegame.
Main Line (c3 + d4 centre).plan: You came out of the opening a clean pawn up with a strong protected passed pawn on d5 and active pieces. From here: keep your pieces active, especially the rook on e4 and knight, support the d5-pawn, and aim to trade down into a winning endgame where that extra pawn tells. Don't rush — your structure is better, so simplify when you can and let the d-pawn become a monster. If Black tries counterplay, just keep your king safe and convert calmly.

Modern Slow Line (d3).name: Modern Slow Line (d3)
notes: 1.e4 — centre, freedom. You know the drill.
1...e5 — the classical reply.
2.Nf3 — develop, attack e5.
2...Nc6 — defend, develop.
3.Bc4 — bishop eyes f7, the Italian signature.
3...Bc5 — mirror match, both bishops loaded.
4.d3 — the 'Pianissimo' (very quiet) move. No fireworks — just a rock-solid build-up. This is what the world's best actually play today.
4...Nf6 — develop and eye e4. Calm and classical.
5.O-O — king to safety first. Patience is the plan.
5...d6 — supports e5 and opens the c8-bishop's diagonal. Solid as concrete.
6.c3 — prep a future d4 and give the bishop a c2 retreat. Tiny move, big plans.
6...a6 — stops Bb5/Nb5 ideas and prepares to keep the bishop. Prophylaxis: stopping their fun before it starts.
7.a4 — grab queenside space and stop Black's …b5. A little land grab.
7...Ba7 — tuck the bishop in the corner, safe but still aimed at the centre.
8.Re1 — rook to e1, backing e4 and lining up the e-file. Quietly useful.
8...O-O — Black castles. Everyone's safe; the real chess starts.
9.Nbd2 — the famous Italian knight tour begins: heading for f1–g3 (or c4). Slow but deadly.
9...Be6 — Black offers to trade off your good bishop and finishes developing.
10.Bxe6 — accept the trade; it hands Black doubled e-pawns. A long-term structural plus for you.
10...fxe6 — Black must recapture this way, accepting the doubled pawns in return for a half-open f-file.
11.b4 — start expanding on the queenside, gaining space and eyeing b5/c4 breaks. This is your side of the board.
11...Qe7 — Black connects the rooks and prepares to use that f-file.
12.Qb3 — pile onto the queenside and hit the weak e6-pawn. You're slowly turning the screws — exactly the Pianissimo dream. Welcome to a long, pleasant squeeze.
Modern Slow Line (d3).plan: This is a slow manoeuvring game and you hold the long-term trumps: Black has doubled e-pawns (e5 and e6) which are permanent weaknesses. Your plan: expand on the queenside with b4–b5, manoeuvre that d2-knight to a great square (f1–g3 hitting f5, or c4 hitting d6/e5), and pile pressure on the weak e6/d6 pawns. Don't open the position carelessly — keep it controlled, improve your worst piece each move, and grind Black down. Black's counterplay is the f-file, so keep f2 defended. Patience wins this.

Evans Gambit Accepted.name: Evans Gambit Accepted
notes: 1.e4 — centre, freedom, the usual.
1...e5 — classical reply.
2.Nf3 — develop, hit e5.
2...Nc6 — defend, develop.
3.Bc4 — bishop locks onto f7.
3...Bc5 — mirror. Both sides loaded.
4.b4!? — THE Evans Gambit. Chuck a pawn at the bishop like 'catch!' The point: lure the bishop away, then grab the centre with tempo. Pure 1800s romance.
4...Bxb4 — Black accepts the gift. Free pawn! (the bill comes later.)
5.c3 — kick the bishop again and prep d4. Buying time with threats — exactly what a gambit needs.
5...Ba5 — the bishop keeps the pressure and stays active. The most flexible retreat.
6.d4 — there it is. Blast the centre open while ahead in development. The pawn was just the cover charge.
6...exd4 — Black grabs again, but the development clock is ticking.
7.O-O — castle and open the floodgates; your rooks and bishops are itching.
7...d6 — Black throws up a wall and gives the king some air. Survival mode.
8.cxd4 — recapture, and now you have a monster centre AND a big development lead for one pawn. A bargain.
8...Bb6 — the bishop drops to a safe diagonal, eyeing your centre.
9.Nc3 — develop with tempo, eyeing d5 and e4. Everyone's coming to the party.
9...Bg4 — Black pins your f3-knight to add pressure on d4 and slow you down.
10.Bb5 — a clever pin-breaker: you pin the c6-knight right back and threaten ideas against Black's king.
10...Kf8 — ugh, Black has to step the king aside (can't castle now). A small triumph for your initiative.
11.Be3 — develop the last bishop, defend d4, and complete your beautiful setup. Every piece is out.
11...Nge7 — Black scrambles to develop and connect. You have a huge, classic Evans Gambit position: full development, big centre, attack brewing — all for a single pawn.
Evans Gambit Accepted.plan: Classic Evans Gambit payoff: you've traded a pawn for a massive lead in development, a big d4+e4 centre, and Black's king stuck on f8 unable to castle. Now ATTACK. Plans: play d5 to open lines and rip the centre, swing a rook to the e- or c-file, and target Black's stranded king. Moves like Qb3/Qd2, Rad1, and a timely d5 or e5 break are your bread and butter. Speed matters — your edge is development, so strike before Black untangles and consolidates. If Black ever manages to castle-by-hand and trade pieces, your pawn deficit starts to matter, so keep the pressure relentless.

Fried Liver Attack.name: Fried Liver Attack
notes: 1.e4 — centre grab.
1...e5 — bold central reply.
2.Nf3 — develop, threaten e5.
2...Nc6 — defend e5.
3.Bc4 — bishop targets f7. Remember that square — it's about to get famous.
3...Nf6 — the Two Knights. Black plays for activity, not safety.
4.Ng5!? — the cheeky knight lunges at f7. Snobs call it a beginner move; the people who've studied it call it a winning attack. It double-hits f7.
4...d5 — Black's only good reply: block the bishop and hit back in the centre.
5.exd5 — grab the pawn and keep the f7 pressure alive.
5...Nxd5?! — the natural recapture, walking into the Fried Liver. (The safe 5...Na5 exists, but where's the fun?)
6.Nxf7!! — the SACRIFICE. The knight smashes f7, giving up a piece to drag the king into the open and hunt it. Frying beginners since the 1600s.
6...Kxf7 — Black almost has to take. The king now stands in the middle of the board in his pyjamas.
7.Qf3+ — check, and it double-attacks the d5-knight. You're winning the piece back with interest.
7...Ke6 — the king must step UP to defend d5. Yes, the king on e6 on move 7. Terrifying but forced.
8.Nc3 — pile another attacker on the pinned d5-knight, developing with menace.
8...Nb4 — Black counterattacks your queen and eyes c2. Active defence — the critical try.
9.Qe4 — keep the d5-knight pinned, defend, and stay aimed at the centre. Cool under fire.
9...c6 — Black shores up the d5-knight with a pawn. Building a fortress around the exposed king.
10.a3 — kick the b4-knight back before it gets ideas about c2.
10...Na6 — the knight retreats to the rim; Black is tied in knots but materially up a piece.
11.d4 — open the centre and bring your last pieces toward the naked king. The bishop on c1 and rooks join in.
11...Nac7 — Black reroutes to defend d5 and e6. White has a ferocious attack and full practical compensation — in real games, defending this with your king on e6 is a nightmare. Hunt the king.
Fried Liver Attack.plan: You sacrificed a knight but Black's king is stuck in the centre on e6 and can never feel safe — that's your whole compensation, so you must ATTACK and not let Black consolidate. Plans: open lines toward the king with d4–d5 breaks, develop every piece with tempo (Bc1, O-O-O, rooks to the centre/e-file), and keep the d5-knight pinned and pressured. Castle queenside fast and throw the whole army at e6. Practically, Black has to find a long series of only-moves to survive, so keep checking, keep threatening, and don't trade queens — the attack is everything. If the king ever escapes to safety and Black untangles, you're down material, so make every move a threat.

Traxler Counterattack.name: Traxler Counterattack
notes: 1.e4 — open the centre.
1...e5 — classical.
2.Nf3 — develop, hit e5.
2...Nc6 — defend.
3.Bc4 — the f7 stare.
3...Nf6 — Two Knights, eyeing e4.
4.Ng5 — White lunges at f7 expecting 4...d5. But Black has a wild surprise…
4...Bc5!? — the TRAXLER. Black ignores the threat to f7 entirely and aims at f2. 'You attack my f7? I'll attack your f2 — and I won't blink first.' Madness, and almost sound.
5.Nxf7 — White takes the bait, forking queen and rook. Looks crushing… watch.
5...Bxf2+!! — Black answers with their OWN sacrifice on f2. Two sacs, two cold kings incoming. The most fun you can have in an opening.
6.Kxf2 — the king grabs the bishop (the critical, greedy try).
6...Nxe4+ — check! Black's pieces flood in with tempo while White's king walks the plank.
7.Kg1 — the king scuttles toward the corner, praying for cover.
7...Qh4 — bring the queen in, threatening nasty stuff on f2 and h2. Black has thrown a bishop at the king and is not sorry.
8.g3 — White tries to block the queen and build a wall.
8...Nxg3! — nope. Black blasts the wall with another sac. Relentless.
9.hxg3 — White takes the knight (basically forced).
9...Qxg3+ — the queen crashes in with check. The attack rolls on.
10.Kf1 — the king dodges to f1, still very nervous.
10...Rf8 — Black brings the LAST piece into the attack, pinning down the f7-knight and opening lines. Every Black piece is now screaming at the king.
11.Qh5 — White desperately tries to trade queens and survive, offering some relief.

11...d5! — Black blasts the centre open to bring the c8-bishop into the assault and refuses to let White breathe. Black has a raging attack and huge practical chances for the sacrificed material. The Traxler: where 'objectively unclear' meets 'absurdly fun.'
Traxler Counterattack.plan: You (as Black) have sacrificed material for a monster attack on White's exposed king — so your entire job is to keep the initiative and never let White untangle or trade into safety. Plans: open more lines with …d5 and …Bg4/…Bf5 to drag the last pieces in, keep the queen active around g3/h2/f2, and bring the rook on f8 and the c8-bishop into the hunt. Avoid trading queens unless it wins material — the attack is your compensation. If White consolidates and trades down, you're worse, so play fast, forcing, and fearless. Calculate the checks and keep White's king on the run.

Max Lange Attack.name: Max Lange Attack
notes: 1.e4 — centre, go.
1...e5 — classical reply.
2.Nf3 — develop, threaten e5.
2...Nc6 — defend.
3.Bc4 — bishop takes aim at f7.
3...Bc5 — Black mirrors.
4.d4!? — White cracks the centre open immediately, gambit-style. Welcome to the Max Lange zone.
4...exd4 — Black takes the pawn.
5.O-O — castle and pour gasoline on the position. You want open lines, fast.
5...Nf6 — Black develops and grabs at e4.
6.e5! — the thematic thrust, kicking the f6-knight and seizing space. Razor-sharp now.
6...d5 — Black hits back, blocking the bishop and trying to untangle.
7.exf6 — grab the knight; the f6-pawn becomes a thorn in Black's position.
7...dxc4 — Black grabs the bishop back. Material's level, the position's on fire.
8.Re1+ — check! The rook swings to the open e-file with tempo. Every move comes with a threat.
8...Be6 — Black blocks with the bishop, the only sensible square.
9.Ng5 — pile onto the pinned e6-bishop. Pieces swarming.
9...Qd5 — Black centralises the queen to defend e6 and hold things together. Gutsy.
10.Nc3 — develop with tempo, hit the queen, add an attacker. The whole army's in.
10...Qf5 — the queen sidesteps and keeps defending e6.
11.Nce4 — reroute the knight to e4, a dream square hitting d6/f6/g5 and supporting the attack. Black is getting squeezed.
11...Bf8 — Black has to grovel: the bishop drops back to defend g7 and the king. Passive but necessary.
12.Nxe6 — White cashes in, smashing the e6-bishop and wrecking Black's structure around the king.
12...fxe6 — Black recaptures, but now has shattered pawns (e6, e6-ish mess) and a draughty king. White has a powerful, lasting attack and the better structure. The Max Lange delivers.
Max Lange Attack.plan: You've broken open Black's kingside and saddled them with a wrecked pawn structure and an exposed king — now press the attack and target those weaknesses. Plans: bring your queen and rooks to the e- and d-files to hammer the loose e6-pawn and the king, keep the strong knight on e4 (it's a beast), and look for the f6-pawn (if still there) as a battering ram. Don't let Black trade queens and consolidate — keep pieces on for the attack. Convert by either mating the stuck king or winning the weak pawns and heading to a better endgame. Precision matters: the Max Lange is sharp for both sides, so calculate carefully before committing.

Hungarian Defense.name: Hungarian Defense
notes: 1.e4 — open the centre.
1...e5 — classical.
2.Nf3 — develop, hit e5.
2...Nc6 — defend.
3.Bc4 — the f7 sniper sets up.
3...Be7 — the Hungarian Defense. Instead of the spicy 3...Bc5 or 3...Nf6, Black just plops the bishop on e7. Modest, solid, drama-free. 'No thanks to your sharp lines,' says Black.
4.d4 — White happily takes the big centre, since Black played it safe.
4...exd4 — Black trades to avoid getting squashed.
5.Nxd4 — recapture with the knight, sitting pretty in the centre.
5...Nf6 — develop and poke e4. A tidy, compact setup.
6.Nc3 — develop, defend e4, eye d5. Healthy.
6...O-O — Black tucks the king away. Safety first.
7.O-O — White castles too. Both kings cozy.
7...d6 — Black props up the centre and frees the c8-bishop. Small but solid.
8.h3 — a useful luft move, stopping any …Bg4 pin before it annoys you.
8...Re8 — rook to the e-file, eyeing e4.
9.Re1 — match it: rook to e1, reinforcing e4 and the e-file. Build-up phase.
9...Bf8 — Black re-routes the bishop to its best diagonal (toward g7) for flexible defence.
10.Bf4 — develop with pressure on d6, a slightly soft spot in Black's camp.
10...Nxd4 — Black trades a pair of knights to ease the slightly cramped position.
11.Qxd4 — recapture with the queen, beautifully centralised. White has more space and a pleasant, risk-free edge; Black is solid but passive. A calm, strategic battle lies ahead.
Hungarian Defense.plan: You have a small but safe space advantage with no weaknesses — this is a 'nurse the edge' position, not a knockout. Plans: use your extra central space to manoeuvre pieces to good squares, keep an eye on Black's slightly weak d6-pawn, and consider expanding with moves like Rad1, Bg3 (pressuring d6), and maybe a later e5 or Nd5 break when well-prepared. Don't overpress — Black's position is solid, so improve slowly and keep control. The plan is to slowly increase pressure and provoke a weakness; if Black sits passively, you can gain space on either wing. Trade into a better endgame if the chance appears.

Scotch Gambit Main.name: Scotch Gambit Main
notes: 1.e4 — centre, freedom.
1...e5 — classical reply.
2.Nf3 — develop and threaten e5.
2...Nc6 — defend.
3.d4!? — the Scotch move order. Crack the centre open on move 3, before even developing the bishop. Aggressive intent, declared early.
3...exd4 — Black takes the pawn.
4.Bc4 — NOW the bishop comes out — Scotch Gambit. You offer the d4-pawn for fast development and an attack on f7.
4...Bc5 — Black develops actively and aims at f2. No playing scared.
5.c3 — offer ANOTHER pawn to blast the centre open and gain time. Gambiteers gonna gambit.
5...dxc3 — Black grabs it (declining is fine too, but free pawns tempt).
6.Nxc3 — recapture, fully developed and ahead in the development race. Two pieces out and a target on f7.
6...d6 — Black builds a shell and opens the light bishop's diagonal.
7.Qb3 — double-attack: the queen joins the bishop glaring at f7. Two attackers on the weak spot — alarm bells.
7...Qd7 — Black defends f7 with the queen, the only tidy way to hold.
8.Ng5 — pile a THIRD attacker on f7. You're going all-in on the classic target.
8...Ne5 — Black blocks the bishop's diagonal with the knight, defending f7 and offering to grab the bishop pair.
9.Bb5 — keep the pin alive and dodge the trade, harassing Black's queen and c6.
9...c6 — Black kicks the bishop and shores up d5/b5.
10.f4! — a strong thrust: kick the e5-knight and open the f-file toward Black's king. The initiative rolls on.
10...Bxg1 — Black grabs the rook in the corner (a desperado), accepting messy complications.
11.Rxg1 — recapture. You've given the exchange but have a raging initiative, open lines, and Black's king stuck in the centre. Full-blooded gambit chaos with you calling the shots.
Scotch Gambit Main.plan: You're down a little material but you have a screaming initiative and Black's king is stuck in the centre — so attack while Black is tangled up. Plans: open lines toward the king with f4–f5 and e-file pressure, keep the queen and bishop aimed at f7/the light squares, and bring the g1-rook into the game fast. Castle queenside if you get the chance to connect rooks and add a third attacker. The key is speed and forcing moves — every move should be a threat so Black never gets to develop and consolidate. If Black manages to trade pieces and untangle the king to safety, the material will start to matter, so don't relent. Calculate the sacrifices; this line rewards bold, accurate attacking play.
